note: Guided stories (docs/civic/insight-and-action-spec.md, docs/civic/editorial-policy.md). Each step's mapState is applied through js/main.js's render: the scenario by id, the drain display, modeled tide gates and the rain experiment. Body text may hold {{tokens}} filled from that run of the model (js/civic/tokens.js); a step with tokens lists the claims that carry their provenance. Checked by node tests/civic-check.mjs.

stories.title: Can high Bay water interfere with Berkeley's storm drainage?
stories.dek: Storm drains carry rain to the Bay. When the Bay is high, the model says water could come back up through them, and rain could have nowhere to go. Two City projects under way could take this on.
stories.locationLabel: West Berkeley, from the Marina to Aquatic Park

steps.heading: Where the Bay meets west Berkeley
steps.body: The map shows west Berkeley at an ordinary high tide, which comes almost every day. Blue is ground the Bay covers over the surface. Orange is ground below that water that the Bay cannot reach over the surface. I-80 runs north to south behind the shoreline, and Aquatic Park's lagoon lies just east of it.
steps.whatChanged: The map shows an ordinary high tide, with the storm drain pathway hidden.
caveats: Bare-earth lidar: the survey removes bridges and raised decks, so I-80 and its ramps can look lower than they are.

steps.heading: A severe storm tide, over the ground
steps.body: Raise the Bay to a severe storm tide, one with about a 1% chance each year at today's sea level. In this model, {{wetLandHa}} ha of Berkeley land is under Bay water that arrives over the ground. Another {{lowLandHa}} ha lies below that level but is cut off from the Bay over the surface (orange).
steps.whatChanged: The water rose from an ordinary high tide to the 100-year storm tide. The drain pathway is still hidden.
caveats: Cut-off ground is not flooded ground. It is below the level, with no surface path from the Bay.

steps.heading: If the outfalls are open, the Bay can come up the drains
steps.body: Storm drains run downhill to outfalls on the Bay. If an outfall has no working tide gate, a high Bay can push water back up the pipes and out of the lowest inlets. The model marks cut-off ground that holds a storm drain inlet in a watershed with a modeled outfall: {{drainLandHa}} ha (teal) could fill this way at this level ({{drainByWatershed}}). This is an upper bound. It assumes every inlet connects to an open outfall and that the tide lasts long enough to fill the pipes.
steps.whatChanged: The drain pathway is now shown, with every outfall modeled open.
caveats: The outfall links are modeled from watershed outlines, not surveyed outfalls (D3).
Pipe connections, capacity, invert elevations and tide duration are ignored (D6).

steps.heading: The same tide with tide gates modeled closed
steps.body: Now assume a working tide gate on every modeled outfall, except Aquatic Park's five tide tubes, which the City keeps open to the tide. Ground that can fill up the drains falls from {{baseDrainLandHa}} ha to {{drainLandHa}} ha. Of what remains, {{aquaticParkDrainHa}} ha drains to the Aquatic Park lagoon. This is a sensitivity test between two assumptions. Which outfalls have gates, and whether they work, is not published, so neither run describes the City's drains as they are today.
steps.whatChanged: Tide gates are modeled closed on every outfall but the Aquatic Park tubes. The numbers compare this with every outfall open.
caveats: Closed gates in the model are not flood protection achieved: they also hold rain in (next step).
A gate on record at design stage, the I-80/Gilman project's flap gate, has not been checked as built (V3).

steps.heading: Rain with nowhere to go
steps.body: A shut gate keeps the Bay out and the rain in. Add a 10-year, 6-hour storm, {{rainDepthIn}} in of rain (NOAA Atlas 14), with all of it unable to drain while the tide holds the outfalls shut. The model pools each watershed's runoff at its lowest inlet: {{rainLandHa}} ha of Berkeley land under pooled rain. It is an illustrative storage experiment. One pool per watershed can overstate the depth at that inlet and miss ponding elsewhere, and the runoff method was made for annual loads, not one storm.
steps.whatChanged: A 10-year, 6-hour rainstorm is added, with tide gates still modeled closed and 100% of the runoff held back.
caveats: "Share that cannot drain" is the reader's assumption, not a measured value (R5).
Runoff share uses the Simple Method beyond the drainage areas it was made for (R3).

steps.heading: What would settle it
steps.body: The model cannot say how Berkeley's drains actually behave at a high tide. That would take what the City has not published: where each outfall is and how high its pipe sits, which outfalls have tide gates and whether they work, and how the pipes connect and how much they carry. It would also take observations at high tides. The City's 2023 work orders show where drains back up in rain (D5), not under a high tide. The City's hydraulic model of its storm drains is being updated now, as part of its Stormwater Master Plan (D11).
steps.whatChanged: Same map as the last step. This step lists the evidence the model lacks.

steps.heading: Two City projects that could take this on
steps.body: The City is updating its Stormwater Master Plan, with a new hydraulic model of the storm drains; the work plan gives January 2024 to December 2026. Its published description does not mention Bay tides or sea level rise. Separately, a state grant funds replacing Aquatic Park's tide tubes. The options below are listed with their tradeoffs; the explorer does not rank them.
steps.whatChanged: Same map. This step lists responses.

steps.heading: Ask the City to plan for high Bay water
steps.body: Both projects are adopted and under way, so their scope can still change. Below is a comment you can copy, edit and send to the Public Works Commission, or read at a City Council meeting. It asks the master plan to test the drains with a high Bay, and asks the new tide tubes to be able to close ahead of a storm tide while still draining rain. This explorer sends nothing.
steps.whatChanged: Same map. This step shows the comment and its status.
caveats: The comment argues for a change; the evidence above supports asking the question, not a particular answer.
Communications to City commissions are public record (D11).
